source.title: Compressed but Compromised? A Study of Jailbreaking in Compressed LLMs
source.citation: Satya Sai Srinath Namburi GNVV et al.
source.authors: Satya Sai Srinath Namburi GNVV; Alex James Boyd; Andrew Warrington

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures refusal-direction changes alongside jailbreak outcomes under compression and argues that the direction is only a partial explanation: some compressed models are vulnerable despite a direction close to the original, while some resistant models show a direction shift. It does not intervene on the direction itself.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the original direction-removal and direction-addition findings, but does not reproduce those interventions. Its own relevant results are qualitative comparisons of refusal-direction deviations and jailbreak outcomes under compression; values for these comparisons are presented in figures, without numerical values in the text.
record.test_reason: The study computes the original paper's refusal direction as a diagnostic tool in compressed Llama-2-7B-Chat and Gemma-7B-Chat. It compares deviations in the selected position and layer (baseline position -1, layer 14; Fig. 3, 5) with GCG and AttentionGCG attack success rates. It never ablates or adds the direction, never measures direction suppression during attacks, and reports no refusal rate under any direction intervention. Its result concerns whether direction shifts explain compression-induced jailbreak vulnerability, a hypothesis from ref [44], not whether the direction mediates refusal. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. More precisely: the authors find refusal-direction changes correlate with compression method but 'might not be causal' for jailbreak vulnerability. Layer-pruned models are vulnerable with a near-baseline direction; low-sparsity pruned models are resistant with a shifted direction. Their main conclusion is about compression: low pruning (10-30%) and quantization up to 4-bit increase jailbreak resistance, while higher compression increases vulnerability.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures refusal-direction deviations in compressed models and compares them with jailbreak outcomes; it does not use the original difference-in-means direction as an ablation or addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Compression method and compression level are reported to affect jailbreak outcomes and the relationship between refusal-direction deviation and vulnerability.

fits_no_version.finding: Under compression, shifts in the selected refusal-direction layer and position do not track jailbreak vulnerability. Low-sparsity unstructured-pruned models resist jailbreaks despite shifted direction selection. Layer-pruned models are vulnerable while direction selection stays near baseline. Shown only qualitatively from figures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changes in refusal-direction location after model compression predict changes in jailbreak robustness (hypothesis of Chhabra & Khalili, arXiv:2504.04215).

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted at Lock-LLM Workshop at NeurIPS 2025
record.problems: For the mechanistic comparison, the relevant results are qualitative and largely figure-based; the paper does not report numerical direction values in the text or intervene on the direction. The main experiments examine only 7B models.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted from figures whose plotted values are not described in the text; the text does not specify per-method or per-condition numerical values for the direction comparisons.

untested.parts: No ablation, no activation addition, no refusal measurement on harmless prompts, and no capability check after a direction intervention.
Does not measure whether GCG or AttentionGCG suppress the direction, and no adversarial training against ablation.
Compressed variants are not tested for direction transfer: the direction is recomputed per model and intervention transfer is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/tests labelling is not supported. The paper cites the V1 ablation and addition results but performs no intervention, and its 'refusal direction' analysis plots deviation of the selected position and layer, not the direction itself. All rows measure compression effects or direction-selection shifts, so they link to no version. Gemma-7B-Chat results (Fig. 4, 5) are not in the rows; they could be added if the compression claim is tracked, but they bear on no version here. No numbers are given in text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate or add the direction, test refusal on harmless requests, or assess general capabilities after a direction intervention. Its compression comparisons do not establish the causal effect of the difference-in-means direction.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or train models against its ablation.
Does not test affine, cone-shaped, or multiple-direction accounts.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
No cross-language, model-variant transfer, or base-to-instruct transfer test.
Does not vary refusal-training methods or timing.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Compare refusal-direction deviations after unstructured pruning with the original model.
rows.measure: Refusal-direction deviation from the original model
rows.value: The refusal directions vary from the original model’s value.
rows.note: The paper reports this qualitative comparison but does not give numerical values in the text. No direction intervention is performed.
rows.check: The measure is the deviation of the selected direction's position and layer from baseline ('Position/Layer Anomalies', Fig. 3a), not the direction vector. It does not measure mediation of refusal, and values are figure-only. The Gemma counterpart (Fig. 5) is omitted.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Compare refusal-direction deviations after layer pruning with the original model.

conditions.value: not stated for the comparison in Section 4.4

rows.measure: Refusal-direction deviation from the original model
rows.value: The refusal direction stays closer to the original model’s value.
rows.note: The paper does not give numerical values in the text. This is a direction comparison, not an ablation or addition test.
rows.check: This is a layer-pruning direction-selection deviation (Fig. 3c), not a test of any version. Values are figure-only; layers pruned are 1-8 in Fig. 3c.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate jailbreak attack success after unstructured pruning.
rows.value: The paper reports ASR for compressed models is lower than for the original model at low sparsity.
rows.note: This measures jailbreak behavior under compression, not the effect of removing or adding the refusal direction.
rows.check: ASR under unstructured pruning measures the compression effect on jailbreak robustness, not refusal-direction mediation. This is the study's own compression result.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate jailbreak attack success after layer pruning.
rows.value: The paper describes layer-pruned models as vulnerable to jailbreak attempts, while reporting that up to 8 pruned layers are similar to the original model on jailbreak attempts.
rows.note: The text gives both a broad statement that layer-pruned models are vulnerable and a more qualified description for up to 8 layers. The direction was not manipulated.
rows.check: ASR under layer pruning measures the compression effect, not any version. Text says up to 8 pruned layers behave 'similar to the original model' on jailbreaks, while Sec 4.4 calls layer-pruned models vulnerable; the internal inconsistency should be noted.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama-2-7B-Chat under unstructured pruning and layer pruning
reader_labels.reason: The paper argues the direction is only a partial explanation: low-sparsity models can be resistant despite a direction shift, and layer-pruned models can be vulnerable despite a direction closer to the original (R1-R4). These observations qualify the direction’s explanatory scope but do not test its causal effect by intervention.
